Risk: climate-zone tagging could be inaccurate or too coarse to be genuinely hyperlocal, undermining the core value proposition; mitigation is starting with a reasonably fine-grained zone system and letting users self-correct their tagged zone. This serves the mission by making the specific, hyperlocal answer easier to find than the generic one, right where gardeners already gather.

pitfalls: Building a standalone gardening app instead of extending Meta's existing Groups strength, underestimating how much the community already exists there
Segmenting gardeners by demographics like age instead of by their actual skill level and what kind of local precision they need

cases.title: Design a product for Uber to help family caregivers arrange rides for aging parents
cases.prompt: Design a new Uber product that lets an adult child, living elsewhere, arrange and manage recurring rides for an aging parent who doesn't use a smartphone confidently. Assume no such product exists today.
context: Uber launched Uber Health in 2018, letting healthcare organizations book non-emergency medical transportation rides for patients.
Uber introduced Teen accounts in 2023, letting a parent set up and monitor a teenager's rides from the parent's own Uber app.
Uber operates in thousands of cities globally, with real-time GPS trip tracking visible to the rider.
assumptions: assumed: the caregiver and the aging parent typically live in different cities, not the same household
assumed: the parent has a phone capable of receiving calls or texts, even if unable to comfortably navigate the Uber app themselves
assumed: rides needed are a mix of recurring (e.g. weekly medical appointments) and occasional, ad hoc requests
followUps: How is this different from Uber Health, which already books rides on behalf of patients?
What's the risk of an aging parent feeling surveilled or infantilized by a caregiver managing their rides remotely?
How would you handle a parent who needs help getting in or out of the vehicle, beyond just arranging the ride itself?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume the caregiver and parent live in different cities, that the parent has a basic phone for calls or texts but isn't comfortable navigating the Uber app itself, and that ride needs are a mix of recurring appointments and occasional ad hoc trips. My plan: since no product exists here yet, I'll build the mission and strategic case from scratch, segment the people involved, map the caregiving journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution, distinguishing this clearly from Uber Health, which serves a different relationship.

Uber's core value is turning 'I need to get somewhere' into a solved problem within minutes, but that value depends entirely on being able to confidently operate the app -- something an aging parent with declining smartphone comfort or memory can't always do, even though their transportation need hasn't gone away. The deeper human need for the caregiver is peace of mind that a parent living far away can still get to the places that matter, without either of them needing to coordinate ride logistics by phone call every single time. My mission statement: 'let distance stop being the reason a parent can't get where they need to go.' Strategically, Uber's existing Teen accounts feature already proves the company can build family-oriented, caregiver-managed ride experiences, and Uber Health proves it can serve non-app-fluent riders through a third party, so this product combines strengths Uber has already validated separately.

Ecosystem players are the aging parent (the rider), the adult child (the caregiver arranging rides), and potentially other local family or professional caregivers. I'd segment caregivers by behaviour: (1) proximity caregivers who live nearby and could drive the parent themselves but want backup options, (2) distance caregivers who live in another city and rely entirely on remote coordination, and (3) crisis-only caregivers who only step in during emergencies or specific events, not regularly. I'd prioritize distance caregivers: they have no local alternative and the highest reach x underserved combination, since proximity caregivers have workarounds and crisis-only caregivers don't need a persistent tool.

Mapping the distance caregiver's journey: their parent has a recurring doctor's appointment, the caregiver calls to confirm the parent remembers, worries whether the parent will actually book a ride correctly (or at all), sometimes ends up calling a local family friend as backup, and only finds out the ride happened after the fact, if at all. The problem isn't 'the parent has no way to get a ride' -- Uber exists and could serve them -- it's that the caregiver has no way to arrange and confirm the ride on the parent's behalf while the parent still experiences a simple, low-friction pickup, so the caregiving burden falls on manual phone coordination and after-the-fact worry. This is a problem, not a need, because it's specific: no caregiver-managed booking and confirmation layer for a parent who can't self-serve the app, prioritized highly since it recurs with every appointment and carries real severity (a missed medical appointment). This ties to the mission because unresolved, this problem means distance remains exactly the barrier to care Uber could otherwise remove.

Three angles: (1) a caregiver-linked account, similar in spirit to Teen accounts, where the caregiver books and pays for rides on the parent's behalf, and the parent simply receives a call or simple text confirming a driver is on the way, with no app interaction required; (2) recurring ride scheduling for standing appointments, set up once by the caregiver and auto-booked going forward with a cancel option; (3) a driver-assist flag for these bookings, requesting the driver confirm the rider is safely in the vehicle before departure, given the segment's higher likelihood of needing a bit more assistance. Plotting impact x effort, the caregiver-linked account with call/text confirmation wins for V1: it most directly matches how Uber already built Teen accounts, requires the parent to do nothing beyond answering a call, and solves the core coordination and confirmation problem, while the driver-assist flag is a valuable but separable addition for later. Risk: a parent could feel surveilled or infantilized by a caregiver managing their rides without their full buy-in; mitigation is requiring the parent's own explicit opt-in to link the account, and always giving them a way to see and control settings themselves, even if they rarely use it. This serves the mission by removing distance as a barrier to care, without removing the parent's own agency over their rides.

pitfalls: Confusing this with Uber Health, which serves organizations booking rides for patients, rather than an individual family member coordinating for a specific parent
Designing a caregiver-controlled experience that leaves the aging parent feeling monitored or without agency, rather than genuinely supported

cases.title: Design a product for Reddit to serve hyperlocal neighborhood communities
cases.prompt: Design a new Reddit product focused specifically on hyperlocal, neighborhood-level communities -- more granular than an existing city-wide subreddit. Assume nothing purpose-built for this exists today.
context: Reddit is organized around topic-based communities called subreddits, some of which are already organized around specific cities.
Reddit went public via an IPO in March 2024.
Reddit's core interaction model is threaded discussion with upvoting and downvoting, rather than a chronological feed.
assumptions: assumed: city-level subreddits today mix hyperlocal neighborhood topics with city-wide news and discussion, diluting genuinely local content
assumed: a meaningful share of city-subreddit members would find neighborhood-level granularity more useful for practical, local questions
assumed: real-world location verification would be needed to keep a neighborhood community credible and locally relevant
followUps: How would you prevent a hyperlocal community from becoming too small to sustain active discussion?
What's the risk of location verification creating a privacy concern for users who prefer Reddit's relative anonymity?
How would this coexist with, rather than cannibalize, existing city-wide subreddits?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume city-level subreddits today mix hyperlocal and city-wide content, diluting truly local discussion, that a meaningful share of members would value neighborhood-level granularity, and that some location verification would be needed for credibility. My plan: build the mission and strategic case for this product from scratch, segment city-subreddit members by behaviour, map the journey of someone with a genuinely local question, then propose a solution while being careful not to cannibalize existing city subreddits.

Reddit's value isn't 'discussion forums,' it's letting people find and trust the opinions of others who've actually dealt with the same specific situation, organized by shared interest rather than by who they already know. For a hyperlocal question -- which plumber to call, whether a specific street is safe at night, what a specific local candidate is actually like -- that same principle applies at a much smaller radius than a whole city, where a city-wide subreddit's answers are often too general to be locally reliable. My mission statement: 'make your actual neighbors' collective knowledge as easy to find as a city's.' Strategically, Reddit's existing subreddit structure, moderation tooling, and threaded discussion format are proven assets that a genuinely new neighborhood app would have to build from nothing, so this should be a natural extension of subreddit mechanics, not a separate product entirely.

Ecosystem players are the neighborhood resident, existing city-subreddit moderators, and Reddit's community infrastructure. I'd segment city-subreddit members by behaviour: (1) city-wide news followers who want broad city discussion and have no particular need for hyperlocal granularity, (2) practical-question askers who post asking for genuinely local recommendations or concerns specific to their block or neighborhood, and (3) local-event organizers who want to coordinate something (a cleanup, a meetup) with people who can realistically show up. I'd prioritize practical-question askers: they have a clear, recurring, currently underserved need, since their posts in a city-wide subreddit often get answers irrelevant to their specific area, making them high-reach and clearly underserved by the current structure.

Mapping a practical-question asker's journey: they post a hyperlocal question in the city subreddit, get a mix of answers from people across the entire city, many of which don't actually apply to their specific neighborhood, and have no reliable way to filter for genuinely nearby respondents. The problem isn't 'no one on Reddit could answer this' -- it's that the current subreddit structure has no way to signal or filter by genuine neighborhood proximity, so a hyperlocal question gets diluted by city-wide noise. This is a problem, not a need, because it's specific: no proximity-aware filtering within existing local subreddits, prioritized highly since hyperlocal questions are frequent in any city subreddit and low answer relevance directly undermines the trust Reddit's whole model depends on. This ties to the mission because if hyperlocal answers aren't reliably local, the core promise of finding people who've dealt with your exact situation breaks down at exactly the scale where it matters most.

Three angles: (1) an opt-in, verified neighborhood tag within existing city subreddits, letting a post be filtered or boosted for members who've verified a nearby location, without fragmenting the community into a separate subreddit; (2) fully separate, auto-created neighborhood-level subreddits nested under a city subreddit, mirroring Reddit's existing subreddit-within-topic structure; (3) a lightweight local-radius Q&A feature, more like a structured local-help board than a full subreddit, for narrowly practical questions. Plotting impact x effort, the opt-in neighborhood tag within existing subreddits wins for V1: it avoids fragmenting already-established, active city communities (a real risk with fully separate subreddits, which could end up too small to sustain discussion), and it's a smaller build than a parallel Q&A product. Risk: location verification could raise privacy concerns for users who value Reddit's relative anonymity; mitigation is keeping verification loose (e.g. neighborhood-level, not exact address) and entirely optional, with unverified users still able to participate in the broader city subreddit as today. This serves the mission by making genuinely local answers findable without asking users to give up the anonymity that draws many of them to Reddit in the first place.

pitfalls: Fragmenting active city subreddits into many small, under-populated neighborhood subreddits that can't sustain discussion
Requiring strict location verification that conflicts with Reddit's relative-anonymity culture and depresses participation

cases.title: Design a product for Canva to serve solo small-business owners running their own marketing
cases.prompt: Design a new Canva product specifically for a solo small-business owner -- like someone running a home bakery or a small local service business -- who does their own marketing with no design background. Assume nothing purpose-built for this segment exists today.
context: Canva offers Canva for Teams (previously Canva for Business), aimed at organizations collaborating on designs.
Canva introduced Magic Studio, a set of AI-powered design tools including text-to-image and background removal, in 2023.
Canva offers a print-on-demand service, letting users order physical prints of designs made in the app.
assumptions: assumed: this owner posts to social media and occasionally needs printed materials (flyers, menus) but has no dedicated marketing budget or team
assumed: this owner already uses Canva's free tier or occasionally browses templates, but doesn't have a consistent visual brand across posts
assumed: this owner's time for design work is limited to short bursts, often in between running the actual business
followUps: How is this different from Canva's existing templates, which already target small businesses to some degree?
What's the risk of over-automating design decisions for someone who still wants some creative control?
How would you keep this simple without making it feel like a stripped-down, lesser version of full Canva?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this owner posts to social media occasionally, sometimes needs printed materials, has no dedicated marketing budget or team, and only has short bursts of time for design work between running the actual business. My plan: build the mission and strategic fit for this product from scratch, segment small-business owners by behaviour, map a specific owner's journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution that respects both their time constraints and their desire for some creative control.

Canva's value isn't 'design tools,' it's letting someone with no design training produce something that looks professionally made, closing the gap between what they can imagine and what they can actually produce. For a solo business owner specifically, the deeper need goes beyond one-off designs -- it's looking consistently credible across every post and flyer, without design consistency becoming a full-time job on top of running the business. My mission statement: 'let a business of one look as put-together as a business with a marketing team.' Strategically, Canva's existing templates, Magic Studio AI tools, and print-on-demand service are exactly the building blocks this segment needs, so this product should package existing strengths around this specific owner's constraints rather than build new capability from scratch.

Ecosystem players are the business owner, their customers who see the marketing output, and Canva's existing template and AI tooling. I'd segment small-business owners by behaviour: (1) template-hunters who search fresh each time they need something, with no consistent look across posts, (2) brand-conscious owners who have a rough sense of their brand colors and style but lack the time to apply it consistently, and (3) delegators who occasionally pay a freelancer for anything beyond the basics. I'd prioritize brand-conscious owners: they already have the intent and a rough brand sense, making them the most winnable segment, and they're underserved because nothing in Canva today locks in their specific brand choices once and applies them automatically across future designs.

Mapping a brand-conscious owner's journey: they need a new social post, search templates fresh, pick one that's close to their style, manually re-enter their logo, colors, and fonts again since nothing remembers their choices from last time, and the result is visually similar but not truly consistent across posts. The problem isn't 'they can't make something that looks good' -- Canva's templates already help with that -- it's that there's no persistent, remembered brand setup that automatically applies across every new design, so consistency depends entirely on the owner's memory and manual re-entry each time. This is a problem, not a need, because it's specific: no persistent brand-kit application by default, prioritized highly since it recurs with every single piece of marketing they make, and inconsistent branding directly undermines the credibility this owner is trying to build. This ties to the mission because looking consistently credible, not just occasionally polished, is exactly what a real marketing team would provide and what's missing here.

Three angles: (1) a one-time, guided brand setup (logo, colors, fonts) that's then automatically pre-applied to every template the owner opens going forward, removing repeated manual entry; (2) an AI-assisted 'match my brand' feature using Magic Studio, generating design variations already styled to the saved brand kit for a given post idea; (3) a simple recurring content calendar suggesting what to post and when, tailored to a small business's typical needs (promotions, seasonal content). Plotting impact x effort, the persistent brand-kit auto-application wins for V1: it's a relatively contained feature building directly on Canva's existing template and brand-kit concepts, and it solves the core consistency problem identified, whereas the content calendar addresses a different problem (what to post, not how it looks) and the AI-matching feature can build on the brand kit once it exists. Risk: over-automating brand application could make the owner feel like they've lost creative control over their own designs; mitigation is keeping every auto-applied choice easily overridable in one tap, never locked in. This serves the mission by making consistent, credible branding the default outcome of using Canva, not an extra effort layered on top.

pitfalls: Building this as a stripped-down, lesser version of full Canva instead of packaging existing strengths (templates, Magic Studio, brand kits) around this segment's real constraint, which is time, not capability
Over-automating design choices in a way that removes the creative control this segment still wants to retain

cases.title: Design a product for Stripe to help independent creators get paid across borders
cases.prompt: Design a new Stripe product specifically for independent creators -- freelancers, newsletter writers, coaches -- who need to get paid by clients and fans in multiple countries, often in different currencies. Assume nothing purpose-built for this segment exists today.
context: Stripe Connect lets platforms and marketplaces route payments to multiple recipients, commonly used by platforms that pay out creators or sellers.
Stripe Atlas, launched in 2016, helps founders incorporate a US company, including creators who want a formal business entity.
Stripe supports processing payments in a large number of currencies and settling payouts to bank accounts in many countries.
assumptions: assumed: this creator has clients or fans in at least a handful of different countries, not a single-market business
assumed: this creator operates as an individual or very small operation, without a finance or accounting team
assumed: currency conversion fees and cross-border payout delays are a meaningful, recurring cost and frustration for this segment
followUps: How is this different from what a creator could already build using Stripe Connect or standard Stripe Checkout directly?
What's the risk of a solo creator getting tangled in cross-border tax complexity that this product can't fully solve for them?
How would you decide which currencies and countries to prioritize supporting first?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this creator has clients or fans in multiple countries, operates solo without a finance team, and that currency conversion fees and payout delays are a real recurring cost for them. My plan: build the mission and strategic fit for this product from scratch, segment creators by their cross-border payment behaviour, map a specific creator's journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution, being clear about how this differs from a creator simply using Stripe's existing building blocks directly today.

Stripe's value isn't 'a payments API,' it's letting someone focus on their actual work instead of becoming an amateur expert in payments, tax, and currency handling just to get paid. For an independent creator with an international audience specifically, the deeper need is being paid reliably and predictably despite complexity (currencies, cross-border fees, timing) that a large company would have a finance team to absorb but a solo creator has to absorb personally. My mission statement: 'let getting paid internationally feel as simple as getting paid locally.' Strategically, Stripe's existing multi-currency processing and payout infrastructure, plus Atlas's experience helping individuals formalize a business, are exactly the strengths this product should package specifically for creators rather than leaving them to piece together Stripe's general-purpose tools themselves.

Ecosystem players are the creator, their international clients or fans, and Stripe's existing payments and Atlas infrastructure. I'd segment creators by behaviour: (1) occasional cross-border earners who get paid internationally rarely and don't mind ad hoc handling, (2) recurring cross-border earners with a steady base of international clients or subscribers who deal with the same friction repeatedly, and (3) scaling creators approaching the complexity of needing a formal business entity and more sophisticated tax handling. I'd prioritize recurring cross-border earners: they experience this friction often enough that a solution has real, repeated value, and they're underserved because Stripe's general tools work for them technically but weren't packaged around their specific, repeated pain.

Mapping a recurring cross-border earner's journey: a client or subscriber pays in their local currency, the creator sees the converted amount land with a fee they didn't clearly anticipate, some payouts take longer to settle than others with no clear pattern, and reconciling what was actually earned versus what arrived becomes a manual, recurring headache with no simple summary view. The problem isn't 'Stripe can't process this payment' -- it can -- it's that there's no creator-facing, simplified layer showing predictable, transparent cross-border earnings and payout timing, so a solo creator has to manually piece together clarity that a finance team would otherwise provide. This is a problem, not a need, because it's specific: no transparent, creator-facing cross-border earnings summary, prioritized highly since it recurs with every international payment and directly affects a creator's ability to trust and plan around their own income. This ties to the mission because unpredictability in something as basic as knowing how much they actually earned undermines the simplicity the mission promises.

Three angles: (1) a creator-facing dashboard showing, per payment, the exact conversion rate applied, fee taken, and expected settlement date upfront, before the money moves, not after; (2) a multi-currency balance feature letting a creator hold earnings in the currency they were paid rather than forcing immediate conversion, converting only when they choose to withdraw; (3) bundling Atlas-style guided incorporation specifically for creators crossing into needing a formal entity, tied contextually to when their cross-border volume crosses a relevant threshold. Plotting impact x effort, the upfront transparency dashboard wins for V1: it directly targets the core problem of unpredictability with primarily a reporting and UI layer on data Stripe already processes, versus the multi-currency balance feature which requires deeper product and possibly regulatory work across many currencies. Risk: this segment could still run into cross-border tax complexity this product can't fully solve, leading to disappointment if expectations aren't set correctly; mitigation is being explicit in-product that this handles payment transparency, not tax advice, with clear signposting to when a creator should seek that separately. This serves the mission by making the money side of international creator work as predictable as it should be, even if it doesn't solve every downstream complexity a creator faces.

pitfalls: Building this as a copy of Stripe Connect's platform-facing tools instead of designing specifically for a solo creator with no technical or finance team to configure it
Overpromising that this solves cross-border tax complexity, when it should be scoped clearly to payment transparency and predictability

cases.title: Design a product for Groww to onboard first-time investors in India's smaller towns
cases.prompt: Design a new Groww product specifically for someone in a smaller Indian town or city who has never invested before and is intimidated by financial jargon and market volatility. Assume nothing purpose-built for this exact segment exists today.
context: Groww started in 2017 as a platform for direct mutual fund investments before expanding into stock trading and other investment products.
Groww is registered with SEBI as a stockbroker and depository participant, subject to Indian securities regulation.
Groww offers educational content within its app aimed at explaining investment concepts to new users.
assumptions: assumed: this first-time investor has stable but modest monthly savings capacity, not a lump sum to invest
assumed: this segment is more comfortable in a regional Indian language than in financial English
assumed: this segment's primary current saving behaviour is a bank recurring deposit or fixed deposit, not any market-linked product
followUps: How would you help this segment overcome fear of market volatility without oversimplifying the real risk involved?
What's the risk of pushing this segment into equity products before they're genuinely ready?
How would your onboarding differ for someone comfortable in English versus someone who isn't?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this investor has modest, stable monthly savings rather than a lump sum, is more comfortable in a regional language than financial English, and currently saves through a bank recurring or fixed deposit rather than anything market-linked. My plan: build the mission and strategic case for this product from scratch, segment this audience by their relationship to risk and unfamiliarity, map a specific first-timer's journey, then propose a solution that respects real market risk rather than oversimplifying it.

Groww's value isn't 'a place to buy mutual funds or stocks,' it's making market-linked investing accessible to people who've been taught, implicitly or explicitly, that markets are risky and not really for people like them. For a first-time investor in a smaller town, the deeper need is permission and confidence -- believing that a small, careful step into investing is safe and legitimate, not a gamble reserved for experts. My mission statement: 'make the first step into investing feel as safe and familiar as opening a bank recurring deposit.' Strategically, Groww's existing direct mutual fund roots, a genuinely simpler product than direct stock trading, and its in-app educational content are strengths this product should build from, rather than leading with the more intimidating stock-trading side of the business.

Ecosystem players are the first-time investor, their family (who may influence or discourage the decision), and Groww's existing education and product infrastructure. I'd segment this audience by behaviour: (1) curious-but-anchored savers who've heard about investing but remain anchored to fixed deposits out of comfort, (2) socially-nudged first-timers who are considering investing because a friend or relative already does, and (3) already-convinced first-timers who've decided to invest but don't know where to start. I'd prioritize curious-but-anchored savers: they represent the largest underserved group, since they have latent interest but a strong behavioural anchor to a familiar, if lower-return, saving habit, whereas already-convinced first-timers are closer to converting regardless of extra help.

Mapping a curious-but-anchored saver's journey: they hear about mutual funds from a coworker or social media, feel some curiosity, open an investment app, encounter jargon (NAV, expense ratio, SIP) presented in English with minimal context, feel out of their depth, and default back to renewing their familiar fixed deposit instead. The problem isn't 'they don't want better returns' -- the curiosity is there -- it's that the on-ramp into a first investment assumes a baseline financial literacy and English comfort this segment doesn't have, so the unfamiliarity itself, not the risk, is what stops them at the very first step. This is a problem, not a need, because it's specific: a literacy and language barrier at the exact moment of first product exposure, prioritized highly since it's the single point where this segment's real latent interest most often dies, and it's a large addressable population given how many first-time investors this describes. This ties to the mission because if the very first step feels unsafe or confusing, no amount of downstream product quality will ever be reached.

Three angles: (1) a regional-language-first onboarding flow, not just translated interface text but concepts explained through familiar comparisons (e.g. explicitly comparing a SIP to a recurring deposit the user already understands); (2) a very small, low-stakes 'starter SIP' product with an explicitly tiny suggested first amount, designed to be a safe, low-regret first step rather than a full-commitment decision; (3) a social-proof feature showing anonymized, aggregated data on how many first-time investors from similar towns have started small SIPs, building confidence through relatable numbers rather than abstract encouragement. Plotting impact x effort, the regional-language-first onboarding using familiar comparisons wins for V1: it directly targets the literacy and language barrier identified as the core problem, and it's a more contained content and localization effort than either the starter-SIP product design or a new social-proof data feature, both of which could layer on afterward. Risk: oversimplifying investment concepts through comparisons to familiar products could understate real market risk and volatility; mitigation is being explicit and honest about how a SIP differs from a fixed deposit (no guaranteed return, market-linked risk) even while using familiar framing to explain the mechanics. This serves the mission by making the first step feel safe and legitimate, without ever implying investing itself is risk-free.

pitfalls: Oversimplifying market risk in the name of accessibility, to the point that a first-time investor doesn't understand they could lose money
Assuming translated interface text alone solves the literacy gap, when the real barrier is unfamiliar financial concepts, not just language

cases.title: Design a product for Rapido to serve outstation, intercity short trips
cases.prompt: Design a new Rapido product for people who need to travel between two nearby towns or cities -- a trip too long for a typical in-city ride but not served well by trains or buses. Assume nothing purpose-built for this exists today.
context: Rapido began as a bike-taxi service in India and has since expanded into auto-rickshaw and cab ride categories.
Rapido operates primarily within Indian cities, matching riders with nearby drivers for point-to-point trips.
India's intercity travel between nearby towns is commonly served by state and private bus operators and, on some routes, local train services.
assumptions: assumed: this outstation trip is in the range of one to three hours by road, connecting two nearby towns or a town and a city
assumed: this rider has some flexibility on exact departure time but wants more certainty on trip timing than a shared bus typically offers
assumed: this segment is price-sensitive relative to a private, full-vehicle intercity cab charter
followUps: How is this different from an intercity cab-charter service that already exists in the market?
What's the risk of driver availability being unpredictable for a longer, less frequent trip type compared to Rapido's core short in-city rides?
How would you price this relative to a bus ticket versus a full private cab?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this trip is one to three hours by road between nearby towns, that the rider has some timing flexibility but wants more certainty than a shared bus offers, and that this segment is price-sensitive relative to a fully private intercity cab charter. My plan: build the mission and strategic case for this product from scratch, segment travelers by behaviour, map a specific traveler's journey, then propose a solution, being clear about how this differs from existing cab-charter services.

Rapido's value isn't 'a way to get a ride,' it's matching people needing to go somewhere with nearby available drivers quickly and affordably, without the overhead of booking a full private vehicle. For someone travelling between nearby towns, that same underlying need exists but currently falls into a gap: too long and specific a route for Rapido's in-city matching, too inconvenient in timing for a shared bus, and too expensive for a fully private cab charter. My mission statement: 'make the trip between two nearby towns as easy to book as a ride across town.' Strategically, Rapido's existing driver network and real-time matching engine, proven at in-city scale, are exactly the assets that make expanding into structured intercity matching more viable than building this from nothing.

Ecosystem players are the traveler, drivers willing to take longer trips, and Rapido's existing matching infrastructure. I'd segment travelers by behaviour: (1) time-sensitive travelers who need to be somewhere at a specific time (a job interview, a family event) and can't risk a bus's unpredictable schedule, (2) cost-conscious regular commuters making the same intercity trip repeatedly (e.g. for work) who want a cheaper-than-charter, more reliable-than-bus option, and (3) occasional travelers making a one-off trip with no strong time pressure. I'd prioritize cost-conscious regular commuters: their trip repeats, making them high-reach in aggregate demand even if each trip is infrequent for the traveler themselves, and they're underserved since neither a bus (unpredictable) nor a private charter (expensive) fits their repeated, budget-conscious need.

Mapping a cost-conscious regular commuter's journey: they need to travel to the nearby town regularly, check the bus schedule which may not align with their timing needs, consider a private cab charter but find it too expensive for a trip they make often, and often settle for either wasted time waiting on a bus or an unaffordable charter on days when timing really matters. The problem isn't 'there's no way to get there' -- buses and charters both exist -- it's that no option combines reasonable cost with reasonable timing certainty for this specific, repeated trip length, leaving this segment to choose between two flawed extremes each time. This is a problem, not a need, because it's specific: a missing mid-cost, mid-certainty option for repeated intercity trips, prioritized highly since it recurs regularly for this segment and the cost of the current tradeoff (time or money) is felt every single trip. This ties to the mission because if the gap between in-city and full intercity charter remains unfilled, this segment's actual travel need never gets a genuinely good answer.

Three angles: (1) a shared-intercity matching product, pairing multiple riders heading the same route around a similar time to split cost, similar in spirit to Rapido's core matching but for a longer route and a defined departure window; (2) a scheduled, single-rider intercity booking option at a fixed price below a full charter, prioritizing timing certainty over cost-sharing; (3) a recurring-route subscription for commuters making the same intercity trip regularly, offering a discounted rate in exchange for booking predictability. Plotting impact x effort, the shared-intercity matching product wins for V1: it most directly extends Rapido's existing core matching strength to a new route length, and it's the option most likely to hit this segment's specific need for cost below a private charter, whereas the recurring-route subscription depends on first proving there's enough repeat demand once the core matching product exists. Risk: driver availability for a longer, less frequent trip type may be unpredictable compared to short in-city rides, risking cancellations; mitigation is starting on a small number of proven, high-demand town-pair routes rather than launching broadly, to concentrate driver supply where it's most likely to be reliable. This serves the mission by giving this segment a genuinely new, better-fitting option rather than forcing a choice between an unpredictable bus and an unaffordable charter.

pitfalls: Positioning this as a direct competitor to full private cab-charter services instead of targeting the specific, underserved cost-and-certainty gap below it
Launching broadly across many town pairs at once instead of concentrating on a small number of high-demand routes where driver supply can be reliable

cases.title: Design a product for Ola to build recurring commuter routes around its electric vehicles
cases.prompt: Design a new Ola product specifically built around electric vehicles for people with a fixed daily commute. Assume no existing Ola product is purpose-built for recurring EV commuting.
context: Ola Electric, a separate but affiliated company to Ola Cabs, manufactures and sells electric scooters in India, and completed a stock market listing in 2024.
Ola operates a large ride-hailing service across Indian cities, historically dominated by petrol and CNG vehicles.
Electric vehicles typically have a limited range per charge and rely on charging infrastructure that is less widespread than fuel stations in many Indian cities.
assumptions: assumed: designing for the ride-hailing (cab) side of Ola's business, matching riders to EV cabs, not the personal-ownership Ola Electric scooter business
assumed: this commuter travels the same route, or a small set of routes, most weekdays
assumed: EV cab supply is currently a smaller share of Ola's total fleet than petrol or CNG vehicles in most cities
followUps: Why would a commuter specifically want an EV ride over a regular Ola ride, beyond environmental preference?
What's the risk of promising EV availability for a recurring commute given limited EV fleet supply and charging constraints?
How does this relate to, or stay separate from, the Ola Electric scooter business?

stages.walkthrough: I'll scope this specifically to Ola's ride-hailing cab business, not the separate Ola Electric scooter business, assume this commuter has a fixed route most weekdays, and assume EV cabs are currently a smaller share of the fleet than petrol or CNG vehicles. My plan: build the mission and strategic case for this product from scratch, segment commuters by their motivation for wanting an EV ride specifically, map a commuter's journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution honest about current EV fleet constraints.

Ola's value isn't 'a ride,' it's reliably getting someone from A to B without owning or maintaining a vehicle themselves -- for a recurring commuter, that reliability has to hold up every single weekday, not just occasionally. For a commuter who specifically wants an EV ride, the deeper need layers environmental or cost-conscious values on top of that same reliability need, and today those two things are in tension since EV availability is less predictable than the broader petrol/CNG fleet. My mission statement: 'make choosing an EV for your daily commute as reliable as choosing any other ride.' Strategically, Ola's affiliation with Ola Electric and its existing large-scale ride-hailing matching engine are strengths a competitor without both an EV manufacturing arm and ride-hailing scale would struggle to combine.

Ecosystem players are the commuter, EV-driving partners, and Ola's fleet and matching systems. I'd segment commuters interested in EV rides by behaviour: (1) environmentally-motivated commuters who actively prefer an EV regardless of small cost or time tradeoffs, (2) cost-motivated commuters drawn to potentially lower EV ride pricing where it exists, and (3) indifferent commuters who'd take an EV if offered but have no strong preference either way. I'd prioritize environmentally-motivated commuters: they have the strongest, most consistent underlying motivation to specifically seek out and stick with an EV option even through early-stage supply constraints, making them the segment most likely to make a new, imperfect product worth using and iterating on.

Mapping an environmentally-motivated commuter's journey: they want to consistently choose an EV for their daily commute, but today's booking flow doesn't let them specify that preference, so they either get a petrol/CNG vehicle by default or have to hope for one, with no way to know in advance whether an EV will be available on their route at their usual time. The problem isn't 'Ola has no EVs' -- Ola Electric and EV cab supply exist -- it's that there's no way for a commuter to express and reliably act on an EV preference for a recurring trip, so their stated preference and their actual daily ride experience are disconnected. This is a problem, not a need, because it's specific: no preference-matching mechanism for EV availability on a recurring route, prioritized moderately given current fleet supply constraints, but still real since every commute is a missed opportunity to serve an expressed preference. This ties to the mission because reliability that ignores a stated EV preference isn't the reliability this specific segment is actually asking for.

Three angles: (1) an EV-preference toggle for recurring commute bookings, matching the commuter to EV supply first when available on their route and time, falling back transparently to a non-EV ride rather than failing the booking; (2) a waitlist-style notification letting a commuter know in advance which of their usual weekly trips are likely to have EV availability, based on historical fleet patterns on that route; (3) route-level EV fleet concentration, deliberately allocating more EV supply to high-density recurring-commute corridors identified from booking data. Plotting impact x effort, the EV-preference toggle with transparent fallback wins for V1: it directly solves the preference-expression gap with a contained booking-flow change, and it's honest about current supply limits rather than overpromising, unlike route-level fleet reallocation which requires deeper operational change. Risk: setting an EV preference but frequently falling back to non-EV rides could feel like a broken promise; mitigation is being explicit in the booking flow about EV availability likelihood before the commuter commits to the preference, managing expectations rather than overselling availability. This serves the mission by making the preference genuinely actionable, even under real supply constraints, rather than a token toggle rarely honored.

pitfalls: Overpromising consistent EV availability given genuinely limited current fleet supply, and failing to manage rider expectations honestly
Conflating this ride-hailing EV product with the separate Ola Electric personal-scooter-ownership business, which serves a different need entirely

cases.title: Design a subscription discovery product for Nykaa's first-time online beauty shoppers
cases.prompt: Design a new Nykaa product for someone who is curious about trying new beauty and skincare products but is overwhelmed by the sheer number of options and unsure what actually suits them. Assume no subscription discovery product exists on Nykaa today.
context: Nykaa is an Indian beauty and personal care e-commerce platform, also operating physical retail stores.
Nykaa expanded into fashion through Nykaa Fashion, launched as a separate vertical in 2018.
Nykaa's platform features customer reviews and ratings on individual products.
assumptions: assumed: this shopper has bought a small number of beauty products online before but doesn't browse confidently across the full catalog
assumed: this shopper's skin type, tone, or hair type meaningfully affects which products would actually suit them
assumed: full-size beauty products carry enough cost that trying several at once to find what works is a real financial deterrent for this shopper
followUps: How would you personalize recommendations without an intrusive, lengthy quiz that this shopper won't bother completing?
What's the risk of a subscription box model conflicting with Nykaa's existing on-demand shopping behaviour?
How would you handle a shopper who dislikes most items in a box, and might churn the subscription entirely?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this shopper has bought a few beauty products online before but doesn't browse confidently, that skin type and tone meaningfully affect what suits them, and that full-size product cost makes trying several new things at once a real financial deterrent. My plan: build the mission and strategic case for this product from scratch, segment beauty shoppers by their relationship to discovery, map this shopper's journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution mindful of how it might interact with Nykaa's existing on-demand shopping habits.

Nykaa's value isn't 'a place to buy beauty products,' it's helping someone put their best face forward with confidence, which depends entirely on actually knowing what works for their specific skin, tone, or hair. For a shopper overwhelmed by choice, the deeper need is a trustworthy way to discover what suits them without expensive trial and error, since guessing wrong with a full-size product is a real cost, not just an inconvenience. My mission statement: 'help someone find what actually works for them, before they have to commit to buying it.' Strategically, Nykaa's existing catalog breadth, reviews, and understanding of product-to-skin-type fit through existing filtering and reviews are the raw materials this discovery product should be built from, rather than treating discovery as an entirely separate problem from the existing catalog.

Ecosystem players are the shopper, the brands whose products get sampled, and Nykaa's existing catalog and review infrastructure. I'd segment beauty shoppers by behaviour: (1) confident routine-shoppers who know their preferred brands and repurchase the same products, (2) overwhelmed explorers who are curious to try new things but freeze when faced with the full catalog's range, and (3) trend-followers who buy based on what's currently popular or promoted, regardless of personal fit. I'd prioritize overwhelmed explorers: they have clear latent demand (curiosity to try new things) but are currently the most underserved, since Nykaa's catalog browsing today assumes a level of confidence in narrowing choices that this segment doesn't have.

Mapping an overwhelmed explorer's journey: they open the app wanting to try something new, like a different foundation shade or a new skincare routine, are met with thousands of products and filters that assume they already know what they're looking for, feel unsure which of many options would actually suit their specific skin, and often close the app without buying anything rather than risk money on a guess. The problem isn't 'Nykaa lacks selection' -- the opposite, it has too much for this segment to navigate confidently -- it's that there's no low-risk way to sample a curated, personally-relevant set of products before committing to full-size purchases, so uncertainty itself blocks the purchase entirely. This is a problem, not a need, because it's specific: no low-cost sampling path matched to personal fit, prioritized highly since it's the exact moment this segment's curiosity dies before ever converting into a purchase, and it likely affects a meaningful share of shoppers new to online beauty buying. This ties to the mission because helping someone find what works for them is impossible if they never get to try it in the first place.

Three angles: (1) a lightweight, short preference quiz (skin type, tone, concerns) feeding a recurring, small discovery box of sample or travel-size products matched to that profile, letting the shopper try before committing to full-size; (2) a one-time, non-subscription 'starter discovery kit' for someone new to a specific category (e.g. skincare), lower commitment than an ongoing subscription; (3) in-app AI-assisted shade or product matching using a photo, without any physical sampling involved. Plotting impact x effort, the recurring discovery box with a short quiz wins for V1: it directly solves the identified problem of low-risk sampling matched to personal fit, and a subscription model creates an ongoing, monetizable relationship rather than a single one-time kit, while being simpler to launch than building photo-based AI matching technology from scratch. Risk: a subscription commitment could conflict with this shopper's existing on-demand, no-commitment shopping habits, risking early churn if a box disappoints; mitigation is making the subscription easy to pause or cancel at any time, and using early feedback on disliked items to immediately improve the next box's matching rather than treating one bad box as an acceptable loss. This serves the mission by turning uncertainty into low-risk discovery, converting curiosity into confident purchases over time rather than losing it at the browsing stage.

pitfalls: Designing a long, detailed onboarding quiz that this segment abandons before ever reaching the product, defeating the purpose of removing friction
Launching only as an ongoing subscription without a lower-commitment option, when this segment's core hesitation is about commitment and risk in the first place
